blocks.text: Livy, book 29: Ten envoys of the Locrians, covered in squalor and rags, while the consuls were sitting in the comitium, holding out the suppliants' emblems, olive branches, as is the custom of the Greeks, prostrated themselves on the ground before the tribunal with tearful cries. Polybius, book 3, on Hannibal crossing the Alps: Οἱ περὶ τὴν δίοδον οἰκοῦντες, συμφρονήσαντες ἐπὶ δόλῳ συνήντων αὐτῷ, θάλλους ἔχοντες, καὶ στεφάνους· [II, 567] τοῦτο γὰρ σχεδὸν πᾶσι τοῖς Βαρβάροις ἐπὶ σύνθημα φιλίας, καθάπερ τὸ κηρύκειον τοῖς Ἕλλησιν. [Hoi peri tēn diodon oikountes, symphronēsantes epi dolō synēntōn autō, thallous echontes, kai stephanous; touto gar schedon pasi tois Barbarois epi synthēma philias, kathaper to kērykeion tois Hellēsin.] The inhabitants along the route, having secretly conspired, come to meet him with branches of green olive and with garlands. For almost everywhere among the barbarians this is a sign of peace and friendship, as the caduceus is among the Greeks. Hence Ovid, Fasti book 1:
With your tresses bound with Actian leaves, come, Peace, and gently visit all the world.

With Actian leaves, that is, of the olive, from whose leaves a crown is woven for Peace. In the same way they hold that Minerva made peace with Neptune crowned with this tree, as Tertullian has it in De corona militis, chapter 13. So all interpret it. But why the olive's leaves are called Actian is not yet clear, and what the commentators offer does not satisfy me. I would therefore rather read frondibus Actaeis, that is, Attic leaves: [col. 33] because the olive is believed to have originated in Attica, which in Greek is called Ἀκτὴ [Aktē], whence the gentile adjective Ἀκταῖος [Aktaios]. Stephanus: Ἀκτὴ, οὕτως ἡ Ἀττικὴ ἐκαλεῖτο [Aktē, houtōs hē Attikē ekaleito]. And a little later: Τὸ ἐθνικὸν Ἀκταῖος καὶ Ἀκταῖα [To ethnikon Aktaios kai Aktaia]. Accordingly, just as Actaean honey is Attic honey in Columella on the garden,
Of Narycian pitch, or the honey of Actaean Hymettus:
so an Actaean olive is an Attic olive. Nonnus, Dionysiaca book 27, line 287:
Ἀκταίης τε γέραιρε φερέπτολιν ὄζον ἐλαίης, [Aktaiēs te geraire pheréptolin ozon elaiēs,]
And honour the city-bearing branch of the Actaean olive. Ausonius, in the Mosella, on the sheatfish:
Whom, as if his back were smeared with Actaean olive oil, I take for a river-dwelling dolphin. — —
Note in passing that in Lucian's Tragopodagra φύλλα ἀκτέας [phylla akteas] is something else, when he says:
Τίνες γὰρ οἵδε βάκτρα νωμᾶντες χεροῖν, Κάρηνα φύλλοις ἀκτέας καταστεφεῖς; [Tines gar hoide baktra nōmantes cheroin, Karēna phyllois akteas katastepheis?]
What crowd is this, who hold staves in their hands, their heads bound with garlands of Actaean leaf?

For there ἀκτέα [aktea] is ἀκτὴ [aktē], that is, sambucus [elder]: the gouty are depicted as binding their heads with its leaves, because elder leaves ποδαγρικοῖς βοηθεῖ μετὰ στέατος ταυρείου, ἢ τραγείου [podagrikois boēthei meta steatos taureiou, ē trageiou]. So Dioscorides; and Pliny not very differently. And Samonicus, in the chapter On driving away gout:

Likewise dwarf elder smeared with goat's tallow. [II, 568] Of the olive I add only this: that even in America the custom had long prevailed that olive branches were held to be a sign of peace. Columbus, Navigat. ch. 103, on a certain American island not far from Hispaniola: On our first arrival thirty young girls came to meet us, who, etc. carried olive branches in their hands, and when they approached the commander, they held out the branches to him as a sign of alliance and peace ^{(2)}.
